question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=2 x + y,\qquad v=- x + y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the lines

$$
\begin{aligned}y &=2 - 2 x,\qquad y=x - 4, \\ y &=5 - 2 x,\qquad y=x + 1.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The supplied map sends $(x,y)$ to $(u,v)$. The area formula uses the absolute determinant of its *inverse*.

$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\iint_\Delta\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm d u\,\mathrm d v.
$$

**Step 1: Map the boundaries.**

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2 - 2 x&\Longrightarrow u=2. \\ y=5 - 2 x&\Longrightarrow u=5. \\ y=x - 4&\Longrightarrow v=-4. \\ y=x + 1&\Longrightarrow v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):2\leq u\leq 5,\quad -4\leq v\leq 1\}.
$$

![The transformed rectangle; the two axes may use different scales.](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186129261/rectangle-04e471c48b11f713da341833d9d3977857fbd9c29dd6fa587958752d7d9085b5.png)

**Step 2: Compute the forward Jacobian.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3: Express the inverse area factor in the new coordinates.**



$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=\frac{1}{3} \\ &=\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$



$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

The affine determinant is nonzero, so the map is one-to-one.

**Step 4: Integrate over the rectangle.**



$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\int_{2}^{5}\int_{-4}^{1}\frac{1}{3}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left[u\right]_{2}^{5}\left[v\right]_{-4}^{1} \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left(5-(2)\right)\left(1-(-4)\right) \\ &=5.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=x y^{2},\qquad v=x^{2} y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{27}{y^{2}},\qquad x=\frac{64}{y^{2}}, \\ y &=\frac{27}{x^{2}},\qquad y=\frac{1}{x^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The supplied map sends $(x,y)$ to $(u,v)$. The area formula uses the absolute determinant of its *inverse*.

$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\iint_\Delta\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm d u\,\mathrm d v.
$$

**Step 1: Map the boundaries.**

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{27}{y^{2}}&\Longrightarrow u=27. \\ x=\frac{64}{y^{2}}&\Longrightarrow u=64. \\ y=\frac{1}{x^{2}}&\Longrightarrow v=1. \\ y=\frac{27}{x^{2}}&\Longrightarrow v=27.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):27\leq u\leq 64,\quad 1\leq v\leq 27\}.
$$

![The transformed rectangle; the two axes may use different scales.](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186129261/rectangle-f39c6a9c0cc4e61da3eb716664acc5262adb9685fd30b0510c2bd22d049162ed.png)

**Step 2: Compute the forward Jacobian.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}y^{2} & 2 x y \\ 2 x y & x^{2}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=- 3 x^{2} y^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3: Express the inverse area factor in the new coordinates.**

Both coordinates are positive. Multiplying the supplied expressions gives

$$
uv=x^3y^3=(xy)^3,\qquad x^2y^2=(uv)^{2/3}.
$$



$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=- \frac{1}{3 x^{2} y^{2}} \\ &=- \frac{1}{3 u^{\frac{2}{3}} v^{\frac{2}{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$



$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\frac{1}{3 u^{\frac{2}{3}} v^{\frac{2}{3}}}.
$$

The positive inverse is unique:

$$
x=\frac{v^{\frac{2}{3}}}{\sqrt[3]{u}},\qquad y=\frac{u^{\frac{2}{3}}}{\sqrt[3]{v}}.
$$

These expressions are defined throughout the positive rectangle, and the determinant never vanishes.

**Step 4: Integrate over the rectangle.**



$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\int_{27}^{64}\int_{1}^{27}\frac{1}{3 u^{\frac{2}{3}} v^{\frac{2}{3}}}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left[3 \sqrt[3]{u}\right]_{27}^{64}\left[3 \sqrt[3]{v}\right]_{1}^{27} \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left(12-(9)\right)\left(9-(3)\right) \\ &=6.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=x y,\qquad v=\frac{y^{2}}{x},
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{y^{2}}{5},\qquad y=\frac{4}{x}, \\ x &=\frac{y^{2}}{3},\qquad y=\frac{2}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The supplied map sends $(x,y)$ to $(u,v)$. The area formula uses the absolute determinant of its *inverse*.

$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\iint_\Delta\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm d u\,\mathrm d v.
$$

**Step 1: Map the boundaries.**

$$
\begin{aligned}y=\frac{2}{x}&\Longrightarrow u=2. \\ y=\frac{4}{x}&\Longrightarrow u=4. \\ x=\frac{y^{2}}{3}&\Longrightarrow v=3. \\ x=\frac{y^{2}}{5}&\Longrightarrow v=5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):2\leq u\leq 4,\quad 3\leq v\leq 5\}.
$$

![The transformed rectangle; the two axes may use different scales.](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186129261/rectangle-13c7db0fad8cf26467f308d6c18699f0e977154c04b37a77e7594c927f706756.png)

**Step 2: Compute the forward Jacobian.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}y & x \\ - \frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}} & \frac{2 y}{x}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\frac{3 y^{2}}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3: Express the inverse area factor in the new coordinates.**



$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=\frac{x}{3 y^{2}} \\ &=\frac{1}{3 v}.\end{aligned}
$$



$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\frac{1}{3 v}.
$$

The positive inverse is unique:

$$
x=\frac{u^{\frac{2}{3}}}{\sqrt[3]{v}},\qquad y=\sqrt[3]{u} \sqrt[3]{v}.
$$

These expressions are defined throughout the positive rectangle, and the determinant never vanishes.

**Step 4: Integrate over the rectangle.**

For the logarithmic endpoint difference, use $\ln A-\ln B=\ln(A/B)$ and $\ln(a^m)=m\ln a$ for positive arguments.

$$
\begin{aligned}\ln 5-\ln 3&=\ln\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)=- \ln{\left(3 \right)} + \ln{\left(5 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$



$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\int_{2}^{4}\int_{3}^{5}\frac{1}{3 v}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left[u\right]_{2}^{4}\left[\ln{\left(v \right)}\right]_{3}^{5} \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left(4-(2)\right)\left(\ln{\left(5 \right)}-(\ln{\left(3 \right)})\right) \\ &=- \frac{2 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{3} + \frac{2 \ln{\left(5 \right)}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4: Integrate over the rectangle.**

For the logarithmic endpoint difference, use $\ln A-\ln B=\ln(A/B)$ and $\ln(a^m)=m\ln a$ for positive arguments.

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=x^{2} y,\qquad v=\frac{1}{x y},
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
\begin{aligned}y &=\frac{1}{5 x},\qquad y=\frac{4}{x^{2}}, \\ y &=\frac{1}{3 x},\qquad y=\frac{2}{x^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The supplied map sends $(x,y)$ to $(u,v)$. The area formula uses the absolute determinant of its *inverse*.

$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\iint_\Delta\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm d u\,\mathrm d v.
$$

**Step 1: Map the boundaries.**

$$
\begin{aligned}y=\frac{2}{x^{2}}&\Longrightarrow u=2. \\ y=\frac{4}{x^{2}}&\Longrightarrow u=4. \\ y=\frac{1}{3 x}&\Longrightarrow v=3. \\ y=\frac{1}{5 x}&\Longrightarrow v=5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):2\leq u\leq 4,\quad 3\leq v\leq 5\}.
$$

![The transformed rectangle; the two axes may use different scales.](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186129261/rectangle-13c7db0fad8cf26467f308d6c18699f0e977154c04b37a77e7594c927f706756.png)

**Step 2: Compute the forward Jacobian.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}2 x y & x^{2} \\ - \frac{1}{x^{2} y} & - \frac{1}{x y^{2}}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=- \frac{1}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3: Express the inverse area factor in the new coordinates.**

The reciprocal simplifies using the supplied products:

$$
y=\frac{(xy)^2}{x^2y}=\frac{1}{v^2u}.
$$



$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=- y \\ &=- \frac{1}{u v^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$



$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\frac{1}{u v^{2}}.
$$

The positive inverse is unique:

$$
x=u v,\qquad y=\frac{1}{u v^{2}}.
$$

These expressions are defined throughout the positive rectangle, and the determinant never vanishes.

**Step 4: Integrate over the rectangle.**

For the logarithmic endpoint difference, use $\ln A-\ln B=\ln(A/B)$ and $\ln(a^m)=m\ln a$ for positive arguments.

$$
\begin{aligned}\ln 4-\ln 2&=\ln\left(\frac{4}{2}\right)=\ln{\left(2 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$



$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\int_{2}^{4}\int_{3}^{5}\frac{1}{u v^{2}}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\ &=1\left[\ln{\left(u \right)}\right]_{2}^{4}\left[- \frac{1}{v}\right]_{3}^{5} \\ &=1\left(2 \ln{\left(2 \right)}-(\ln{\left(2 \right)})\right)\left(- \frac{1}{5}-\left(- \frac{1}{3}\right)\right) \\ &=\frac{2 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{y^{2}}{x},\qquad v=\frac{y}{x^{2}},
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
\begin{aligned}y &=5 x^{2},\qquad x=\frac{y^{2}}{4}, \\ y &=3 x^{2},\qquad x=\frac{y^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The supplied map sends $(x,y)$ to $(u,v)$. The area formula uses the absolute determinant of its *inverse*.

$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\iint_\Delta\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,\mathrm d u\,\mathrm d v.
$$

**Step 1: Map the boundaries.**

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{y^{2}}{2}&\Longrightarrow u=2. \\ x=\frac{y^{2}}{4}&\Longrightarrow u=4. \\ y=3 x^{2}&\Longrightarrow v=3. \\ y=5 x^{2}&\Longrightarrow v=5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):2\leq u\leq 4,\quad 3\leq v\leq 5\}.
$$

![The transformed rectangle; the two axes may use different scales.](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186129261/rectangle-13c7db0fad8cf26467f308d6c18699f0e977154c04b37a77e7594c927f706756.png)

**Step 2: Compute the forward Jacobian.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}- \frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}} & \frac{2 y}{x} \\ - \frac{2 y}{x^{3}} & \frac{1}{x^{2}}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\frac{3 y^{2}}{x^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3: Express the inverse area factor in the new coordinates.**



$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}&=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1} \\ &=\frac{x^{4}}{3 y^{2}} \\ &=\frac{1}{3 v^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$



$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\frac{1}{3 v^{2}}.
$$

The positive inverse is unique:

$$
x=\frac{\sqrt[3]{u}}{v^{\frac{2}{3}}},\qquad y=\frac{u^{\frac{2}{3}}}{\sqrt[3]{v}}.
$$

These expressions are defined throughout the positive rectangle, and the determinant never vanishes.

**Step 4: Integrate over the rectangle.**



$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\int_{2}^{4}\int_{3}^{5}\frac{1}{3 v^{2}}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left[u\right]_{2}^{4}\left[- \frac{1}{v}\right]_{3}^{5} \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\left(4-(2)\right)\left(- \frac{1}{5}-\left(- \frac{1}{3}\right)\right) \\ &=\frac{4}{45}.\end{aligned}
$$
